notes: Make (make.com, formerly Integromat, founded in Prague and acquired by Celonis in 2020) has not published a fixed numbered list of 'Leadership Principles' the way Amazon has. The 'leadership_principles_behavioral' dimension below is instead built around recurring themes in how Make publicly describes its mission and product philosophy (see worker/src/prompts.ts's MAKE_VALUES and its source comments) — candidates should be evaluated on whether their story genuinely demonstrates one of these themes, not on reciting an official slogan.
1 = very weak / almost no evidence; 3 = moderate / acceptable; 5 = very strong / model answer.
Feedback tone: strict but constructive, like a coach who genuinely wants you to get the offer.

product_sense.name: Product Sense / Product Design
question_examples: Design a way for a non-technical Make user to understand why a complex scenario with 10+ modules failed silently.
How would you improve the experience of discovering the right modules/apps when someone is building their first scenario?

clarity_and_structure.description: Whether the answer has clear assumptions, a game plan, and a clearly segmented structure (framing how they'll break down the problem up front, rather than jumping straight to a solution).
good_signals: Opens by restating the problem, clarifying goals and constraints, and making explicit assumptions where needed.
States their process up front, e.g.: user first, then pain points, then solution + metrics.
Every paragraph has a clear topic sentence with natural transitions.
bad_signals: Jumps straight into listing solutions or features with no framing at all.
Rambles with no paragraph structure, reads like stream of consciousness.
Never signals which part of the answer they're currently in (e.g. user, problem, solution).

scoring_guide.1: No structure at all — the answer is scattered and hard to follow.
scoring_guide.3: Has basic structure but inconsistent — some sections are clear, others jump around.
scoring_guide.5: Clearly structured throughout, like walking the interviewer through a design process step by step.

customer_obsession_and_motivation.description: Whether the answer explains why this product/problem matters starting from the user — for Make, specifically the non-technical 'creator' building a workflow themselves rather than waiting on engineering, which is the core of how Make describes its own mission ('empower creators to innovate without limits').
good_signals: Clearly describes the situation, skill level, and pain points of a specific type of Make user (e.g. an ops person automating a manual process, a solo founder, an agency building for clients) rather than a generic 'users'.
Connects concrete behavior and frustration with framing like 'If I were this creator staring at a failed scenario, what I'd need most is...'.
Ties back to Make's positioning as more powerful than a pure no-code tool but more accessible than writing code — the answer respects that the user isn't a developer.
bad_signals: Starts purely from a technical/engineering angle with no discussion of the non-technical creator's experience at all.
Uses vague language like 'make it easier' without defining what's actually hard today.
Assumes the user has the same mental model as someone who builds the platform itself.

scoring_guide.1: Barely mentions the user, or only in very generic terms.
scoring_guide.3: Has basic user framing but not concrete or situational enough.
scoring_guide.5: Genuinely feels like they understand a specific type of Make creator's workflow and concrete frustrations.

segmentation_and_focus.description: Whether users/use cases are reasonably segmented, and whether the candidate picks one clear focus to go deep on — relevant for Make since its user base spans solo no-code beginners, power users doing complex multi-branch scenarios, and enterprise teams on Make ONE.
good_signals: Lists several possible user segments (e.g. first-time creator, power user, agency, enterprise admin) and explains why their needs differ.
Clearly picks one primary segment and explains why (impact, fit, underserved).
All subsequent problem framing and solutioning stays aimed at that segment, without drifting to others.
bad_signals: The whole answer talks about 'all Make users' with no real focus.
Segments are defined too superficially (e.g. only by plan tier) without connecting to skill level and motivation.
Keeps switching the target audience mid-answer, so the story falls apart.

scoring_guide.1: No segmentation at all — fully one-size-fits-all.
scoring_guide.3: Some segmentation attempted but unclear, or the reasoning for the chosen focus is weak.
scoring_guide.5: Segments are clear and mutually exclusive, and the answer stays consistently focused on the chosen one.

problem_identification.description: Whether the candidate genuinely understands and concretely describes the user's problem to solve, rather than jumping straight to a feature.
good_signals: Describes the pain point with a concrete scenario, e.g. exactly where in the scenario-building or debugging flow a creator gets stuck.
Distinguishes between a 'want/wish' and an actual 'blocker' (e.g. 'more integrations' vs. 'can't tell which module in a 15-step scenario failed').
Connects the problem to its impact (e.g. abandoned scenario builds, support tickets, churn before upgrading from free).
bad_signals: Treats a feature request as the problem itself, e.g. 'there's no debugging panel, so we need one'.
Describes the problem too abstractly to imagine happening to a real creator.
Lists a pile of problems with no prioritization.

scoring_guide.1: Doesn't show what specific problem is actually being solved.
scoring_guide.3: Lists a few reasonable problems, but not deep enough or unprioritized.
scoring_guide.5: Problem is concrete and prioritized, and directly drives the design decisions that follow.

solution_quality_and_tradeoffs.description: Whether the proposed solution has enough depth, a clearly scoped v1, and trade-offs that fit Make's visual-first, accessible-but-powerful product philosophy.
good_signals: States the high-level solution direction first, then breaks it into a few key experience/feature modules.
Clearly defines v1 vs. future extensions, showing judgment about what to ship first.
Calls out risks and downsides (e.g. adding a feature that makes the visual canvas more cluttered), and explains how to mitigate them.
bad_signals: Throws out ideas like a feature list with no connection or prioritization.
v1 tries to do too much, unrealistic given resources and time-to-value.
Never mentions any risk, failure mode, or constraint — e.g. ignores that added complexity could hurt the platform's core promise of accessibility.

scoring_guide.1: Solution is scattered or clearly unrealistic.
scoring_guide.3: Has a roughly reasonable direction, but v1 scope / trade-offs are unclear.
scoring_guide.5: Proposes a convincing, practical v1 and clearly explains why it's designed that way.

analytical_execution.name: Analytical / Execution / Metrics
question_examples: Make's activation metric is roughly 'ran a scenario successfully for the first time.' How would you improve it?
A cohort of free-trial users is churning before upgrading to a paid plan. How would you investigate why?

goal_definition.description: Whether the candidate clearly defines what goal or success state the problem is meant to achieve.
good_signals: Clearly distinguishes input vs. output metrics.
Asks up front, 'What are we actually trying to optimize for — activation, retention, expansion revenue?'.
Connects back to Make's business model: a freemium, credit/operations-based platform where usage growth and plan upgrades both matter.
bad_signals: Jumps straight into listing KPIs without explaining why they're the right ones.
Fixates on a single metric with no consideration of balance or side effects.
Never addresses the relationship between activation and longer-term retention/expansion.

metric_selection_and_reasoning.description: Which metrics are chosen, why, and whether there are guardrail metrics.
good_signals: Proposes 1-2 north star metrics paired with 3-5 supporting/guardrail metrics.
Explains what creator behavior each metric represents (e.g. scenarios published, modules connected, error rate on active scenarios).
Considers trade-offs, e.g. encouraging more scenario creation vs. keeping operations/credit usage sustainable for the user.
bad_signals: Piles on metrics arbitrarily with no prioritization.
Chosen metrics aren't actually measurable or aren't related to the problem.
Forgets qualitative/behavioral metrics related to whether the automation actually works reliably.

structured_debugging_and_hypotheses.description: When facing an anomalous metric, whether the candidate systematically hypothesizes causes and designs ways to validate them.
good_signals: First distinguishes whether this is a tracking issue vs. a real behavior change.
Hypothesizes in layers (onboarding friction / pricing confusion / missing an integration they need / a competitor).
Proposes concrete experiments or analysis methods to validate (funnel breakdown, cohort analysis, user interviews with churned trial users).
bad_signals: Guesses at causes purely on intuition with no systematic breakdown.
Forgets to rule out instrumentation/logging errors.
Never proposes any concrete way to validate a hypothesis.

prioritization_and_tradeoffs.description: Given multiple possible solutions or experiments, whether there's a clear prioritization.
good_signals: Prioritizes using an impact vs. effort/risk framing.
Accounts for resource constraints rather than greedily trying to do everything at once.
Explains why a given experiment goes first, and what the next step is if it fails.
bad_signals: Treats every idea as equally high priority.
Doesn't consider execution cost or technical risk.
Picks their favorite idea with no clear reasoning.

leadership_principles_behavioral.name: Leadership Principles / Behavioral
question_examples: Tell me about a time you built something that let a non-technical person solve their own problem without waiting on engineering.
Describe a time you simplified something complex for a user without dumbing it down or removing real power.

story_structure_star.description: Whether the story is told clearly using a STAR / STAR+ structure, rather than a rambling description.
good_signals: Clearly states Situation / Task / Action / Result, ideally with a Reflection as well.
Every part has a clear timeline and clearly defined roles.
The result is concrete, with numbers or an observable change.
bad_signals: Everything is blended together — unclear what the problem was, what they did, and what the result was.
The result is vague, e.g. 'everyone was happy' with no concrete evidence.
The story is too short or shallow, like routine day-to-day work.

ownership_and_decision_making.description: Whether the candidate shows accountability for outcomes and proactively elevated their perspective to make decisions, rather than just executing instructions.
good_signals: Clearly states they proactively identified the problem or proposed the solution, rather than being assigned it.
Explains their own role in the key decision, including the risk and consequences they owned.
Pushed back / exercised influence when facing resistance, rather than passively accepting it.
bad_signals: The whole story sounds like they were just following someone else's plan.
Blames the problem or failure entirely on other people or circumstances.
No evidence of long-term thinking anywhere in the story.

alignment_with_specific_lp.description: Whether the story actually demonstrates a specific Make theme (e.g. Creator Empowerment, Radical Simplicity, Practical Power — see worker/src/prompts.ts's MAKE_VALUES), rather than just claiming 'this shows X'.
good_signals: The action details themselves show the theme in practice, e.g. for Radical Simplicity, concretely describing how they hid complexity from an end user without removing capability.
Connects to the spirit of the theme, rather than just reciting a label.
Reiterates the lesson learned in the result or reflection section.
bad_signals: Only says 'this is empowerment' at the start or end of the story, with no evidence in the middle.
Crams in too many themes at once, so each one is weakly supported.
The story content actually contradicts the claimed theme, e.g. claiming Radical Simplicity while the whole story is about adding more configuration options.

reflection_and_learning.description: Whether there's genuine reflection on the experience, and an explanation of how behavior changed afterward.
good_signals: Admits there were things they could have done better, not afraid to name a real misstep.
States a concrete, observable behavior change (e.g. how they'd design the escape hatch for power users earlier next time).
Ties the reflection back to a broader lesson about building for non-technical users, or career growth.
bad_signals: The 'lesson learned' is vague, e.g. 'communicate more'.
No reflection at all — just showcasing success.
The reflection is unrelated to the actual story.

strategy_business.name: Strategy / Business Thinking
question_examples: Zapier has a much larger app ecosystem and a more polished UX; n8n is open-source, self-hostable, and developer-loved. How should Make differentiate and win?
Should Make prioritize going further upmarket to compete with Workato and Tray.ai in the enterprise segment, or stay focused on the prosumer/SMB middle tier?

structured_market_and_customer_analysis.description: Whether market, competition, and customers are analyzed in a structured way, rather than just a pile of buzzwords.
good_signals: Starts by roughly scoping the market (TAM/SAM/SOM is fine at a rough level) across the iPaaS/automation space.
Clearly describes the differences and needs across target customer groups (solo/prosumer, SMB, mid-market, enterprise).
Identifies key competitors/alternatives (Zapier, n8n, Workato, Tray.ai, Microsoft Power Automate) and Make's relative strengths and weaknesses.
bad_signals: Just says the market is big or growing fast, with no structure at all.
Ignores Make's existing capabilities and position, as if this were a brand-new startup with no users.
Recites business-school frameworks with no real connection to Make's actual context.

make_ecosystem_and_platform_fit.description: Whether the strategy accounts for how Make's own growth loop actually works: more integrations and shared templates let more non-technical creators solve more of their own problems, which drives more usage and community-built content, which attracts more app partners to build official integrations. Also whether it accounts for Make's position as a business unit within Celonis (process mining/execution management), which is a real, distinctive asset most pure-play automation competitors don't have.
good_signals: Discusses how the strategy affects the integration count, template/community ecosystem, and ease of building a first working scenario.
Explains how this strategy reinforces (or is reinforced by) Make's relationship with Celonis, its EU-native infrastructure/data-residency positioning, or its AI Agents/MCP direction.
Considers the impact on third-party app partners and the creator community, not just end users.
bad_signals: The strategy could apply to any automation company — nothing about Make's specific position (mid-tier between Zapier's ease and code-first tools, Celonis-owned, EU-native) is addressed.
Ignores the ecosystem/partner side entirely, only talks about end users.
Only discusses short-term revenue, no consideration of long-term platform trust and the creator community.

prioritization_and_roadmapping.description: Whether the strategy can be broken down into an actionable roadmap with a clear sequence.
good_signals: Proposes 2-3 main strategic directions, each broken into milestones or initiatives.
Accounts for resource constraints and risk, clearly stating what comes first and what comes later.
Describes how each strategic direction's success would be tracked with metrics.
bad_signals: Stays very high-level with no concrete execution steps at all.
The 'roadmap' is just a timeline with no real strategic thread connecting it.
Ignores risks and dependencies.

estimation.name: Estimation / Guesstimate
question_examples: Estimate how many scenarios are actively running (scheduled or triggered) on Make's platform at any given moment.
Estimate how many of Make's active users build at least one scenario that uses an AI module (OpenAI/Claude/Gemini) within their first month.

assumption_clarity.description: Whether every assumption made is clearly stated, and whether the candidate checks that it's reasonable.
good_signals: States the key assumptions (active user count, scenarios per user, run frequency, etc.) before calculating.
Assumptions are logically consistent with each other, not contradictory.
Willing to adjust an assumption when needed, and explains why.
bad_signals: Throws out numbers with no stated source.
Realizes partway through that an earlier assumption was wrong, but doesn't fix it.
An assumption is clearly unreasonable (e.g. every free user runs 10,000 scenario executions a day).

problem_breakdown_and_math.description: Whether the problem is reasonably broken down and the math comes out roughly correct.
good_signals: Breaks the big problem into a few dimensions (active users x scenarios per user x runs per scenario per day, etc.).
The calculation process is orderly and clearly narrated out loud.
Sanity-checks the final result to see if it looks reasonable.
bad_signals: The breakdown is disorganized or double-counts the same group of users.
Gets lost partway through without reorganizing the steps.
No sanity check at all.

communication_and_poise.description: Whether the candidate stays calm and clear while estimating out loud, and how they handle uncertainty.
good_signals: Narrates their thinking while calculating, so the interviewer can follow along.
When uncertain, is willing to say 'there are two ways to break this down, I'll go with this one first'.
Doesn't get thrown off entirely by a small mistake.
bad_signals: Panics the moment a calculation error is noticed, and the whole answer falls apart.
Never verbalizes their thought process, so it's unclear how they're thinking.
Obsesses over precise decimal points, losing sight of the big picture.

system_design.name: System Design / TPM
question_examples: Design the execution engine that reliably runs millions of scheduled/triggered automation scenarios, including retry and error handling.
Design how a Make AI Agent could safely modify a running scenario without breaking other scenarios that depend on it.

requirements_and_scoping.description: Whether the candidate clarifies functional and non-functional requirements (scale, latency, consistency, who the users are) before proposing a design, rather than designing in a vacuum.
good_signals: Asks about scale (scenarios/day, concurrent executions), latency expectations, and consistency needs up front.
Clarifies which use cases are in scope for v1 vs later (e.g. simple linear scenarios vs. complex router/iterator branching).
States explicit assumptions when the interviewer doesn't provide a number.
bad_signals: Jumps straight into naming technologies/components with no sense of scale or constraints.
Never distinguishes must-have requirements from nice-to-haves.
Ignores who actually uses the system and why (non-technical creators depending on scenarios running unattended in production).

high_level_architecture.description: Whether the candidate proposes a clear, sensible breakdown of the system into major components and explains how data/requests flow between them.
good_signals: Breaks the system into a small number of clear components (e.g. trigger/scheduler, execution engine, module connectors, error handling/retry queue) with a simple story for how they connect.
Explains the role of each component in plain language before naming any specific technology.
Keeps the design at the right altitude for a PM/TPM — enough structure to reason about trade-offs, not a line-by-line engineering spec.
bad_signals: Describes components with no explanation of how they interact.
Gets lost in low-level implementation detail (specific algorithms, exact schemas) instead of the overall shape.
The design doesn't actually address the stated requirements.

scalability_and_tradeoffs.description: Whether the candidate identifies where the design would break under scale and reasons about real trade-offs (e.g. consistency vs. availability, cost vs. latency, build vs. buy).
good_signals: Identifies the most likely bottleneck (e.g. a hot queue during a traffic spike, a slow third-party API a scenario depends on) and proposes a fix.
Explicitly names a trade-off and picks a side with a reason, rather than listing pros/cons with no decision.
Considers cost (Make's own credit/operations-based pricing model implies real infrastructure cost per execution) and engineering effort, not just theoretical scalability.
bad_signals: Treats the system as if it will always run at small scale with no failure modes.
Lists trade-offs without ever committing to a recommendation.
Adds complexity without justifying why it's needed.

operational_and_cross_team_thinking.description: Whether the candidate addresses how the system would be monitored, rolled out safely, and delivered in practice — including working with engineering and other teams, which is central to the TPM angle of this question type.
good_signals: Mentions how they'd monitor health (key metrics/alerts, e.g. scenario failure rate) and detect failures after launch.
Describes a staged rollout (e.g. internal dogfood, small percentage, then full launch) rather than a single big-bang release.
Talks about which teams (engineering, data, ops, and given Make's Prague-based product/eng org, potentially Celonis-side security/infra teams) need to be involved and where dependencies or risks lie.
bad_signals: The design ends at launch with no mention of what happens operationally afterward.
No acknowledgment that other teams or dependencies exist.
Ignores failure handling entirely, as if the system will never go down.

ai_pm.name: AI Product Manager
question_examples: Design the product experience for Make AI Agents — how would you help a non-technical creator go from a simple deterministic workflow to an adaptive AI agent without hitting a wall of complexity?
How would you decide when a scenario should offer an 'AI agent' step versus a simple deterministic module?

problem_ml_fit.description: Whether the candidate first establishes that the problem genuinely calls for an AI/agentic solution — and what that solution needs to be good at — rather than assuming AI is the answer by default, which matters a lot for Make given it offers both deterministic scenarios and AI Agents as distinct product surfaces.
good_signals: Asks what a deterministic (non-agentic) scenario would look like and explains concretely why an adaptive AI agent does better here — e.g. the decision logic is too variable to hard-code as routers/filters.
Identifies what the agent actually needs to decide or generate, in plain language, before discussing models or architecture.
Considers user trust and explainability implications of handing decision-making to an AI agent inside a production automation.
bad_signals: Assumes 'add an AI agent' is the answer without explaining what problem it solves better than a deterministic scenario.
Confuses the AI feature with the product goal, e.g. treats 'add an agent step' as the goal itself.
Never considers whether a simpler, faster-to-ship deterministic solution would work almost as well.

data_and_evaluation_strategy.description: Whether the candidate thinks concretely about what data/context the agent needs and how they would measure whether it's actually working, both offline and after launch.
good_signals: Names the specific context/tools (e.g. via MCP, connected modules) the agent needs and where they'd realistically come from.

Proposes concrete offline metrics (e.g. task success rate on a benchmark set of scenarios) AND online/business metrics (e.g. scenario completion without human intervention), and explains why both matter.
Considers what 'good enough to ship' looks like, not just 'best possible agent'.
bad_signals: Never mentions evaluation at all, as if the agent works perfectly out of the box.
Picks a single vague metric like 'accuracy' with no connection to the business or creator outcome.
Confuses model-quality metrics with product success metrics, or never distinguishes them.

responsible_ai_and_risk.description: Whether the candidate proactively considers failure modes, and safety risks the AI feature could introduce given it runs inside unattended production automations, and how to guard against them.
good_signals: Names a concrete failure mode specific to this feature (e.g. an agent taking an unintended action against a connected app, like sending an email or deleting a record).

Proposes a concrete guardrail: scoped permissions per connected app, a human-in-the-loop approval step for high-risk actions, or a way to catch bad agent decisions before they reach a customer's real systems.
Considers creator trust and how a visible agent mistake in a production scenario would affect it.
bad_signals: Treats the agent as if it will never make a wrong decision.
Mentions 'responsible AI' only as a buzzword with no concrete mechanism.
Ignores the specific risk profile of agentic automation acting on real connected business systems.

iteration_and_feedback_loops.description: Whether the candidate describes a realistic plan for launching, monitoring, and improving the AI feature over time, including how model drift and user feedback are handled.
good_signals: Describes a staged launch (e.g. shadow mode, small percentage rollout, opt-in beta with the community) before a full launch.
Explains how they'd detect the agent degrading over time (drift, changing connected-app behavior) after launch.
Describes a concrete feedback loop, e.g. using creator corrections or explicit feedback to improve agent prompting/tooling.
bad_signals: Treats the launch as the finish line with no plan for what happens after.
Never mentions how they'd know if the agent gets worse over time.
No mechanism for turning real-world usage back into agent improvement.
